genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a neighborhood drop-in center
she grew up next door to a noisy workshop
quarrels between neighbors marked her childhood
she decided to face conflicts instead of avoiding them
she began by listing what people argued about
she set up a weekly drop-in session
so many people came that the room grew too small
the local council granted her a larger space
she credits her experience rather than any inborn gift
text: From a glass-walled office looking onto the courtyard, the woman who runs the neighborhood drop-in center watches families come and go. Her method makes sense once you know her history. As a child she lived in an apartment that shared a wall with a noisy workshop, and the quarrels between neighbors left a lasting mark on her. Grown up, she chose to deal with conflict rather than walk away from it. She knew those everyday grudges from the inside, so she began by listing what people argued about, then opened a drop-in session once a week. Families poured in by the second week, and the room quickly grew too small. That turnout persuaded the local council to hand over a much larger space next door. None of it comes from any inborn gift, she says. She simply turned an old wound into a useful skill.

units: the covered hall was remodeled recently
the designers wanted one open volume with no partitions
the din of the stalls disturbs those who come to read
children moving about unsettle people looking for quiet
thick hangings on rails now divide the space
these dividers can be moved as needs change
the fix cost little and built nothing permanent
the writer prefers this correction to the original design
text: Walking into the remodeled covered hall feels like entering a sentence that never comes to an end: the eye hunts for something to rest on and finds nothing to hold it. The flaw shows itself at the threshold, well before you have crossed the first aisle. The designers wanted one continuous volume, no partitions anywhere, every use blending softly into the next. Instead the din of the stalls swallows the readers sitting at the back, and children weaving between the tables unsettle anyone who came in looking for quiet. What has been done since deserves praise. Nothing heavy was built. Thick hangings on rails now cut the nave into rooms, and they slide along to wherever the day requires. The place breathes at last. It gains in warmth what it loses in purity, and that owned-up flaw beats the fine idea that made the building unlivable.

units: the writer compares two waste collection systems
the first system gives each dwelling its own bin
this first system is expensive to maintain
it makes sorting mistakes traceable
the second system is a shared container sunk below ground
this container costs less and keeps the smell in
its anonymity encourages illegal dumping
the writer recommends the second system with clear signage
the decision will be made at an upcoming residents meeting
text: Here is my answer about the two sorting systems our building is weighing up. The first gives every apartment its own bin, emptied once a week by the contractor. Upkeep runs high, but it keeps each household honest, since a sorting mistake can be traced back to a door. The second costs far less: everything goes into one shared container sunk below ground, on the strip of land beside the parking area. It holds plenty, and the lid keeps the smell in. The trouble is that nobody can be identified, so people dump whatever they like. Compare them and it comes down to this. One fixes habits, the other fixes clutter. Since bags piling up by the entrance is our real headache, I lean toward the buried container, provided we add signage anyone can read. Tell me what you think before the residents meeting.

units: the head of an urban services department is asked about public consultation
she believes consultation exposes uses that clash
three topics come up at almost every meeting
people living on the street want traffic slowed
shopkeepers fear losing customers
noise complaints run against the need for places open late
terraces cut into the room left for people on foot
the department head denies that consultation settles disputes
the final decision belongs to the elected representatives
text: Asked what a public consultation is really good for, the head of the urban services department answers that it brings clashing uses out into the open. Three themes surface at nearly every meeting she attends, she notes. The first one is traffic: people living along the street want it slowed down, while the shopkeepers fear their customers will drift away for good. The second concerns the hours after dark, where she sets the need for somewhere young people can go late against the steady complaints about noise. The third is the sidewalk, where the terraces eat into the room left for strollers and for wheelchairs. Does the consultation settle these disputes? She says plainly that it does not. It gives them a shape, sorts them by weight, and then hands the burden of choosing to the elected representatives.

units: the president of an association asks a volunteer about the state of the lobby
the volunteer reports overflowing mailboxes and parcels on the floor
the caretaker has been out sick for two weeks
no stand-in was arranged
a tenant had already reported it in writing without any reply
the treasurer suggests paying for a temporary replacement
the tenant objects that the fund is meant for something else
the president decides to visit the apartments the next day
a general meeting will be called if nobody steps forward
text: Near the end of the meeting, the president of the association asked the young volunteer what exactly he had seen in the lobby. The mailboxes were overflowing, the volunteer said, and parcels had been sitting there on the floor since the day before. The president wanted to know what lay behind such an unusual mess. The caretaker had been out sick for two weeks, the volunteer explained, and nobody at all had taken over his rounds. A tenant spoke up from the back: she had already reported the whole thing in writing and had never heard back. The treasurer offered to pay for a stand-in, just this once. The tenant objected that the money was set aside for something else entirely. The president settled it there. He would knock on every door the next day, and call a general meeting if no one stepped forward.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: streets did not carry posted names from the start
people once found their way by shop signs and trades
this worked as long as the neighborhood stayed small
the spread of the outskirts made spoken directions useless
the authorities could no longer collect the taxes
they could no longer find the people they were after
numbering the housefronts grew out of this trouble
the mail carrier daily round follows from it as well
residents pushed back against the measure at first
they saw it as an intrusion into their private life
text: Believe it or not, streets did not start out with their names posted on a plate. People found their way by painted signs and shopfronts. You lived by the well, or across from the tanner, and that did the job as long as the whole neighborhood fit into a handful of lanes. Then the outskirts spread, newcomers arrived in crowds, and directions passed along by word of mouth stopped working. The authorities reacted for a very practical reason. They could no longer collect the taxes, and they could no longer put their hands on the people they were after. That is where numbers on housefronts come from, and the mail carrier daily round along with them. The odd part is that residents pushed back at first. An address handed to them felt like a stranger walking into their private life.

units: a rumor of a break-in spreads through a residents group chat
the message is twisted and blown up in one evening
an alarming story travels faster than a denial
fear makes people warn those close to them
setting the record straight takes patient checking
some neighborhood groups appoint two verifiers
these verifiers check every alert before it goes out
a waiting period is imposed before anything is shared
the number of alerts drops and trust climbs back
text: A rumor swells inside the residents group chat: intruders got into the basement. Within a single evening the message has been passed on, twisted, and blown out of all proportion. Researchers who study how information travels know the pattern well. An alarming story outruns any denial, because it feeds on fear, and fear makes each of us warn the people we care about. One message is enough to put a whole building on edge, while setting the record straight takes slow and patient checking. Some neighborhood groups are trying out a fix that actually works. They name two people whose job is to verify every alert before it goes out, and they impose a waiting period before anything at all is shared. The result comes as a surprise. Alerts drop off, trust climbs back, and the exchanges turn useful again.

units: the narrator watches two lines form in a single week
the first stands at an administrative counter
this first line stays silent and packed tight
everyone in it keeps an eye on the spot they hold
the second waits outside a community canteen
people there talk loudly
they hold the place of a neighbor who has stepped away
the difference comes neither from the wait nor from the weather
it comes from what each person hopes for at the end of the line
text: I came across two crowds in the same week, and they had nothing in common. The first was waiting at an administrative counter: packed tight, silent, shuffling under an awning too short to cover anyone. Each person kept an eye on the spot he had. Nothing passed between them but sighs and sideways looks, as though waiting there ruled out speech. The second had formed outside a community canteen open to all. It shuffled just as much, under the same drizzle, but voices carried, and someone would hold a place for the neighbor who had stepped away for an umbrella. The gap had nothing to do with the wait or the weather. It came from what each person hoped for at the end of the line. At the counter they feared a refusal. At the canteen they expected hot soup and a familiar face.

units: the procedure applies before a community space opens to the public
measure the width of the entrance door
check the slope of the ramp
a wheelchair must turn without awkward maneuvering
the emergency exits must be located and cleared
the charge on the extinguishers and the electrical inspection must be verified
the furniture must be entered in a register with its condition
seats that sag under weight must be pulled out
a felt panel cures the echo of a bare ceiling
the compliance papers must be requested from the owner after a renovation
text: Before you open a community space to the public, run these checks in order. Start with access: measure the width of the entrance door, check the slope of the ramp, and make sure a wheelchair can turn without awkward maneuvering. Move on to safety. Locate the emergency exits, clear whatever blocks them, and verify the charge on the extinguishers along with the inspection of the electrical panel. Then handle the furniture: enter every chair and table in a register, note the condition of each, and pull out any seat that sags under weight. Finish with sound, which people tend to forget. A bare ceiling throws voices back and makes talking tiring, while a felt panel is enough to cure it. If the building has been renovated lately, ask the owner for the compliance papers and file them with the register.

units: a job placement association asked to occupy an idle warehouse
the warehouse belongs to a public housing landlord
the request drew no reply at first
a technical meeting brought together the landlord the safety services and the people behind the project
the project planned a repair workshop and a shared kitchen
the experts required the roof structure to be reinforced
the landlord agreed to pay for the bracing
the association pledged to handle upkeep and keep watch over the place
the agreement was signed at the end of autumn
a building next door is now the subject of a similar request
text: It began when a job placement association applied for temporary use of an idle warehouse owned by a public housing landlord. The request drew no reply at first. Two weeks later, a technical meeting brought the landlord together with the safety services and the people behind the project, who wanted to put a repair workshop and a shared kitchen under that roof. The experts concluded that the roof structure had to be reinforced, and that without it the doors could not open to the public. The landlord put forward a compromise. It would pay for the bracing, while the association would handle day-to-day upkeep and keep watch over the place. The agreement was signed at the end of autumn. The workshop has opened since, and the idle building next door is now the subject of a similar request.
